item.title: Cosmic Evolution Survey: LOFAR 144 MHz imaging of the COSMOS field
item.description: arXiv:2610.18648v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We present the first deep, targeted LOFAR 144 MHz source catalogue of the COSMOS field, together with the first 144 MHz source counts in this field. The data comprise 48 h of observations. Over the 2.6 sq. deg. region adopted for the catalogue analysis, the final Dutch-array image reaches a median rms sensitivity of ~100 uJy/beam at an angular resolution of 15" x 6". The resulting catalogue contains 1984 radio sources; a peak S/N >= 5 selection is adopted for the resolved/unresolved classification and source-count analysis. We characterised the catalogue using Monte Carlo source-injection and recovery simulations, including dedicated simulations of extended sources, to quantify completeness, flux-density redistribution, and morphology-dependent source-recovery effects. The catalogue reaches 90% completeness at 1.48 mJy. The resulting Euclidean-normalised differential source counts are measured down to ~0.4 mJy and show good agreement with LoTSS DR3 144 MHz source counts and with the VLA-COSMOS 3 GHz counts scaled to 144 MHz, with ~5% of catalogue sources having multiple 3 GHz counterparts within a beam-matched search region. Comparison with the VLA-COSMOS 3 GHz catalogue shows good astrometric agreement, with median offsets of Delta_RA = 0.35" (+0.03"/-0.05") and Delta_Dec = -0.83" (+0.02"/-0.03"), approximately 6% of the corresponding synthesised-beam dimensions, and no significant radial dependence across the field. The resulting catalogue provides a low-frequency view of COSMOS and a reference dataset for future deeper LOFAR observations and multiwavelength studies of this extensively characterised extragalactic field.

item.title: The Connection Between the Growth of Massive Black Holes and Their Dynamical Histories
item.description: arXiv:2610.18659v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Massive black holes (MBHs) grow through both gas accretion and mergers and it remains unclear how variations to MBH growth and dynamical histories contribute to the spread in empirical scaling relations between MBHs and their host galaxies. We examine the ex- and in-situ growth of MBHs within large-scale cosmological simulations and compare the evolution of an outlier population of under-grown MBHs to the general population. We use the Romulus25 uniform volume cosmological simulation and the RomulusC cluster zoom-in simulation to examine the growth and merger histories of MBHs. We identify central MBHs that are undergrown relative to other MBHs in similar mass galaxies and investigate their accretion, merger, and orbital histories within the simulations. The contribution of ex-situ growth increases with MBH mass, with mergers becoming increasingly important in the most massive galaxies. We find no difference between cluster and field environments in terms of the importance of ex-situ growth, which is generally very low. Under-grown MBHs have experienced fewer mergers and have had complex dynamical histories, spending significant time 'drifting' within the galaxy or 'competing' with another MBH. Other under-grown MBHs have experienced a 'late entrance' into a galaxy which until then had no central MBH. Our results demonstrate that MBH assembly is dominated by in-situ growth, which in turn is impacted by the dynamical histories of MBHs within assembling galaxies. Prolonged off-centre evolution can suppress accretion and contribute to the formation of under-grown central MBHs at $z=0$.

item.title: A Spectroscopic Census of Cluster White Dwarfs from DESI, LAMOST, and SDSS
item.description: arXiv:2610.14166v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Gaia has substantially expanded the sample of candidate white dwarfs (WDs) in open clusters, but many remain without spectroscopic characterization. We leverage the increasingly extensive archives of large public spectroscopic surveys to identify 62 candidate cluster WDs with available spectra from DESI, LAMOST, and SDSS. After discarding sources with very low S/N and unreliable host clusters, 44 candidates remain, including 37 non-magnetic DA WDs, of which 15 had not previously been characterized in the literature for cluster studies. We find that nine are consistent with single-star origins in their proposed host clusters, increasing the combined cluster DA initial--final mass relation (IFMR) sample to 132 WDs. All lie within $2\sigma$ of the best-fit IFMR from the most comprehensive recent cluster WD sample, suggesting these additions do not require recalibrating the empirical IFMR. One is a likely Hyades tidal-tail WD, providing further evidence that dynamical dispersal helps explain the long-standing WD deficit in the nearest cluster. We further compare WDs with spectra from multiple surveys. Among seven Praesepe WDs observed by both DESI and SDSS, DESI gives higher WD masses in six cases, with a mean difference of $0.067\,\mathrm{M}_\odot$, while the inferred progenitor masses differ by as much as $0.459\,\mathrm{M}_\odot$. More broadly, nine of ten single-star cluster DAs with DESI spectra lie above the empirical IFMR, with a mean final-mass residual of $0.06\pm0.04\,\mathrm{M}_\odot$. These results show that survey-dependent differences can strongly affect cluster WD parameters, and should be considered when combining heterogeneous spectroscopy in empirical IFMR studies.

item.title: Where Cluster Galaxies Reside and How Strongly They Lens
item.description: arXiv:2610.14167v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: The efficiency of galaxy-galaxy strong lensing (GGSL) in clusters depends jointly on the inner mass distributions of member galaxies and their locations within the cluster potential. Observed GGSL probabilities exceed $\Lambda$CDM predictions by nearly an order of magnitude, but the relative roles of internal structure and environment remain unclear. We disentangle these effects by comparing HST strong-lensing clusters with TNG-Cluster analogs at similar lens redshifts, matched by their primary Einstein radius. For each member, we measure its lensing strength in isolation and when embedded in the cluster field. Members in cluster-critical regions are classified as Major or Minor Perturbers depending on whether they strongly lens in isolation; those in subcritical regions are classified as Intrinsic Lenses, Boosted Lenses, or Inert Members according to whether they lens independently, only with environmental assistance, or not at all. Observed clusters contain 33.7% of selected members in cluster-critical regions, compared with 21.6% in TNG-Cluster, while their Major-to-Minor ratios are similar. Outside these regions, observations contain substantially more Intrinsic and Boosted Lenses and fewer Inert Members, with Boosted Lens fractions of 25.8% and 13.5%, respectively. The discrepancy persists at fixed subhalo mass and after including line-of-sight structure. A mass-conserving contraction mimicking core-collapsed self-interacting dark matter largely recovers the conditional lensing fractions but not cluster-critical occupancy. The GGSL discrepancy therefore reflects both insufficient central concentration in simulated members and differences in their locations within the cluster lensing field.

item.title: The $R$-Process Alliance: On J0010$-$1735, an Accreted, Chemically Unusual, Metal-poor Star with $R$-process Enhancement
item.description: arXiv:2610.14987v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We present a detailed chemo-dynamical analysis of the chemically peculiar very metal-poor ([Fe/H]$=-2.22\pm 0.11$) Milky Way (MW) halo star, 2MASS J00101758$-$1735387 (hereafter J0010-1735), discovered by the $R$-Process Alliance. We derive abundances for 45 elements, including 28 neutron-capture elements, and confirm that \thestar\ is highly $r$-process-enhanced, with [Eu/Fe]=$+1.30$. The light, $\alpha$, and Fe-peak element abundances ratios relative to Fe are all sub-solar, aside from C, Si, and most extremely, Ca. We investigate three possible formation scenarios based on the star's chemical abundances and orbital kinematics: whether it formed in the \textit{in-situ} MW halo, in a MW dwarf galaxy satellite, or in a satellite of the Magellanic Cloud system. Using the position of \thestar\ in the [Mg/Mn]--[Al/Fe] plane, the abundance pattern of both the light and heavy elements, and the kinematics, we conclude that J0010-1735 most plausibly originated in a now-disrupted ultra-faint dwarf galaxy that was accreted into the MW halo. We examine potential chemical enrichment scenarios of J0010-1735, including one similar to the $r$-process-enhanced UFD Reticulum II, or enrichment via a sub-Chandrasekhar Type Ia SNe, potentially supplemented by a Ca-rich gap transient and by a separate neutron-rich site that facilitated $r$-process enrichment. A nuclear cosmochronometric age of $12.5\pm4.2$ Gyr is derived from the [Th/Eu] ratio, consistent with an ancient origin in one of the earliest star-forming systems in the universe.

item.title: An asteroseismic age estimate for the Pleiades using a neural-network emulator of rotating $\delta$ Scuti pulsation models
item.description: arXiv:2610.15939v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Asteroseismology of $\delta$ Sct stars has strong potential for determining the ages of young stars through individual mode fitting. We present a neural-network emulator trained on approximately 46 million rotating pulsation models. From stellar mass, metallicity, age, and equatorial rotation velocity, it predicts 12 classical observables, two asteroseismic scalars, and the p mode, f mode and low-order g mode frequencies for degrees $\ell=0$-3, including the individual $m$ components of rotationally split multiplets. We couple the emulator to nested sampling through a multivariate likelihood that propagates correlated emulator residuals, making full Bayesian posterior exploration practical. Applied to five $\delta$ Sct stars in the Pleiades observed by TESS, the framework gives mutually consistent individual asteroseismic ages of 107-117 Myr. Combining their age posteriors gives a cluster age of $113.3\pm4.5$ Myr (statistical), consistent with the $112 \pm 5$ Myr lithium-depletion-boundary age and the 110-160 Myr range from rotating-isochrone fitting. Together with spectroscopic $v\sin i$, the inferred equatorial velocities also provide post-fit inclination estimates. Separate perturbed-grid tests using 100 matched synthetic pairs per input-physics variation give median absolute age shifts of $2.1$, $2.3$, and $5.2$ Myr for $|\Delta f_{\rm ov}|=0.005$, $|\Delta\alpha_{\rm MLT}|=0.1$, and $|\Delta Y|=0.02$, respectively; the corresponding 90th percentile shifts are $6.5$, $7.6$, and $16.2$ Myr. These tests describe conditional population sensitivities, not a systematic uncertainty on the Pleiades age. Together, the cluster-age agreement and the scale of these input-physics sensitivities support $\delta$ Sct asteroseismology as a complementary age estimation method for young stars.

item.title: Blackbody evolution and circumstellar medium properties of broad-lined H-rich superluminous supernovae
item.description: arXiv:2610.16527v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Broad-lined H-rich superluminous supernovae (SLSNe II) tend to show signs of interaction, including a UV excess compared to a blackbody function. However, a quantitative analysis of the CSM configuration and the UV excess has so far not been performed for most of the literature sample. Additionally, SN 2023gpw showed signs of asymmetry in its peculiar blackbody and spectral evolution, raising the question of whether similar properties can be found in other SLSNe II. We aim to characterize the circumstellar environment of SLSNe II by searching for signs of asymmetry, quantifying the UV excess, and investigating any IR echoes produced by dust. Diversity among SLSNe II is also explored. We fit blackbody functions to the SEDs of SLSNe II to quantify the UV excess luminosity and its evolution. We use this to investigate mass-loss rates required to produce the excess through interaction. We also investigate the line profiles in SLSN II at late times and compare line velocities to the blackbody radius evolution. We examine public WISE IR images and place constraints on IR echoes. We find mass loss rates of $\sim10^{-4}$ to $\sim0.03\, \mathrm{M_\odot}$~yr$^{-1}$ when assuming all interaction luminosity emerges in the UV, i.e., conservative lower limits for the total mass loss rate. Radii calculated from line velocities in late-time spectra are mostly too large for a spherical interaction photosphere, only compatible with the blackbody radius evolution if the CSM is non-spherical with a low filling factor. This is in some cases supported by a mismatch between spectroscopic and blackbody expansion velocities. Considerable diversity is seen in the sample, probably as a result of different viewing angles and CSM masses. WISE images seem too shallow to observe IR echoes in SLSNe II beyond $z\sim0.1$, but in the nearest event, SN 2020jhm, a likely IR echo is detected, suggesting pre-existing dust.

item.title: Indirect Dark Matter Detection in the Multi-Messenger Era: Experiments, Systematics, Anomalies, and Prospects for Discovery
item.description: arXiv:2610.17013v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Indirect searches for dark matter (DM) span gamma rays, charged cosmic rays, neutrinos, X-rays, radio emission, the cosmic microwave background (CMB), and the 21~cm signal, but reported constraints and anomalies vary in evidential strength. This critical review synthesizes peer-reviewed literature from January 2000 through October 2026 using a structured search strategy. We assess observations through a framework linking particle interactions and halo source terms to propagation or cosmological energy deposition, instrumental response, background modeling, and statistical inference. Fermi-LAT observations of dwarf spheroidal galaxies provide robust GeV-scale benchmarks for DM annihilation, whereas Galactic-center searches offer higher expected signals but depend more on foregrounds and halo profiles. Charged-cosmic-ray measurements are precise but limited by propagation and source uncertainties, while neutrino searches offer complementary sensitivity through solar capture, directional and flavor information, and high-mass annihilation or decay. Several widely discussed signals, including the 3.5~keV line, 511~keV emission, the Galactic-center GeV excess, charged-particle features, cluster radio excesses, and candidate gamma-ray lines remain inconclusive because of limited independent confirmation, uncertain target scaling, spectral degeneracies, or background-modeling limitations. Cosmological observations provide complementary constraints from CMB energy-injection limits and 21~cm measurements of the intergalactic medium. Artificial intelligence increasingly supports reconstruction and inference but requires rigorous calibration and domain-shift validation. The strongest case for DM discovery would require statistically consistent evidence across independent targets, instruments, or messengers, under common particle-physics parameters, and with well-characterized uncertainties.

item.title: The Cosmic Radio Dipole and Observer Effects in SKA all-sky surveys
item.description: arXiv:2610.17022v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: The Square Kilometre Array (SKA) will observe our Universe on the largest scales and so enable the study of fundamental assumptions in cosmology, such as cosmic homogeneity and isotropy. Observations over recent years have reaffirmed an unexpected challenge to the Cosmological Principle first seen in measurements of the cosmic radio dipole. This dipole anisotropy is thought to be caused by our local observer motion, however, it is observed to be about three times larger than predicted, with significances exceeding 5$\sigma$. The SKA is in a unique position to shed light on this anomaly by measuring this and other effects related to our observer motion. To quantify this, we forecast the capability of large-angle HI and continuum surveys of the SKA to constrain the kinematic matter dipole in galaxy number counts, the modulation of the matter power spectrum by a kinematic dipole, and kinematic spectral distortions of diffuse radio emission.

item.title: Extinction by non-spherical particles with the Nanoparticle Transition Matrix Code: perspectives for interstellar medium and exoplanetary atmospheres
item.description: arXiv:2610.17081v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: The Transition Matrix formalism (T-matrix) offers an optimal solution to the problem of radiation scattering and absorption by particles characterized by a high degree of chemical and structural complexity. However, its application to particle models composed by large numbers of constituents has been classically limited by the substantial computational burden of the method. As a consequence, the investigation of light scattering and absorption processes, in cases where particle asymmetry and non-homogeneity play an important role, typically need to rely on simplifying assumptions which affect the correct interpretation of transmission spectra and extinction curves. This problem has a huge impact on many fields of scientific application. In particular, it has a critical role in astrophysics, because the ability to model highly non homogeneous particles is a fundamental requirement to understand the role of extinction in different phases of the interstellar medium (ISM), as well as to probe the physics of light transmission in planetary atmospheres within the Solar System and beyond. In this work we describe the application of a new implementation of the T-matrix formalism, based on the framework originally developed by Borghese, Denti & Saija and named Nano-particle Transition Matrix code, which leverages the power of modern hardware architectures to reduce the computational costs related to the solution of relevant particle models for the investigation of dust in the ISM and of hot-Jupyter class planets atmospheric aerosols. This new implementation of the T-matrix formalism can handle calculations of increasing complexity with a direct impact in the interpretation of the transmission spectra of transiting exoplanets produced by the James Webb Space Telescope (JWST) and of those expected from the Atmospheric Remote-sensing Infrared Exoplanet Large survey (ARIEL).

item.title: The nearby Type II supernova 2024ggi beyond 600 days: circumstellar interaction and dust formation
item.description: arXiv:2610.17140v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: The Type II SN 2024ggi is one of the nearest core-collapse SNe to have exploded in recent decades. Its proximity has enabled extensive multiwavelength monitoring from early times through the nebular phase. Signatures of late-time interaction between the SN ejecta and hydrogen-rich circumstellar material (CSM) have recently been reported. Here we extend its study using late-time optical photometry and spectroscopy from 570 to 820 d after explosion. We investigate the emergence and evolution of late-time ejecta-CSM interaction and constrain the geometry of the interaction region and the properties of newly formed dust. Comparisons with other interacting SNe II and with synthetic spectra are presented. We model the H$\alpha$ profile with the Monte Carlo radiative-transfer code Damocles, including both gas and dust components. Spectroscopic signatures of interaction precede the photometric flattening. The spectra evolve from ejecta-dominated to interaction-dominated as H$\alpha$ develops a broad, boxy profile. The optical light curves subsequently flatten relative to the $^{56}$Co decay rate at approximately 650-670 d. The emission lines show a systematic blue-to-red asymmetry that requires a dust component newly formed within the ejecta. The inferred dust mass formed in the ejecta is $10^{-6}-10^{-5}$ M$_\odot$ if the grains are amorphous carbon or a carbon-silicate mixture, but can reach up to $10^{-3}$ M$_\odot$ for pure silicates.

item.title: Interpreting the stacked kinetic SZ signal II: the degeneracy between satellite galaxies and baryonic feedback
item.description: arXiv:2610.17200v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: The kinetic Sunyaev-Zel'dovich (kSZ) signal stacked around a galaxy sample traces the gas around halos and is a powerful probe of baryonic feedback. Its interpretation, however, depends on the satellite galaxies in the sample. Using the FLAMINGO hydrodynamical simulations and DESI-like samples of luminous red galaxies (LRGs), bright galaxies survey (BGS), and emission-line galaxies (ELGs), we show that satellites and feedback have similar effects: both suppress the small-scale signal. This degeneracy arises because stacking on satellites, which are offset from the centre of their host haloes, mimics the extended gas distribution produced by feedback. Although satellites make up only 20-30% of each sample, they account for 50-80% of the signal because they occupy more massive halos than centrals; thus their imprint on the stacked profiles can be as large as that of feedback. At the precision of current DESI$\times$ACT data, neglecting satellites in the modelling biases the inferred gas fractions low, by up to a factor of two, and overestimates the feedback strength, particularly for the LRG and BGS samples. Remaining agnostic about the satellite population avoids this bias but reduces the constraining power, so robust constraints would require knowing the satellite fraction to better than 10%, for instance from lensing and clustering data of the same galaxy samples. Finally, a further contribution from satellites will become statistically significant with upcoming surveys: satellites trace the anisotropic gas distribution around their host haloes, an effect that contributes 10% of the signal, and will likely require simulation-based models to capture.

item.title: MRI Turbulence versus $\alpha$-Viscosity in Circumbinary Disks: Implications for Gravitational-Wave Dephasing and Accretion Variability
item.description: arXiv:2610.17212v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Our understanding of gas torques on massive black hole binaries (MBHBs) relies on hydrodynamical (HD) simulations of circumbinary disks (CBDs) in which an $\alpha$-viscosity models angular momentum transport. However, CBDs around MBHBs near merger are hot, magnetized plasmas where transport is driven by magnetohydrodynamical (MHD) turbulence sustained by the magnetorotational instability (MRI). We test how well an $\alpha$-viscosity captures MRI turbulence with 3D global Athena++ simulations of a locally isothermal CBD around an equal-mass, circular MBHB, run in HD and MHD from the same initial torus on identical grids, so that only the transport mechanism differs. Excising the region within twice the binary separation, $r<2~a_{\rm bin}$, allows $1000$ orbits of evolution, several times longer than previous MHD simulations. Both disks deliver the same accretion rate, and the gas beyond $2~a_{\rm bin}$ exerts a positive torque in both, yet the MHD torque is $3.5$ times larger and $3$ times more variable. Near the midplane, transport is similar in the disk body but three times weaker in MHD at the cavity edge, where $2$-$3$ times more mass piles up in a more eccentric cavity, raising the torque. The accretion rate is modulated mainly at twice the binary frequency in HD, but by a persistent lump at the cavity edge and its beat with the binary in MHD. The outer-disk torque therefore implies a contribution to the gas-induced phase shift in the gravitational-wave signal of LISA binaries $3.5$ times larger than in $\alpha$-disk models, and a different variability signature for LSST and Roman.

item.title: From Giant Envelopes to Rapidly Contracting Cores in Rotating Population III Stars from $500$ to $1000 \, M_\odot$
item.description: arXiv:2610.17218v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Population III (Pop III) stars link the chemical enrichment of the early Universe to the formation of the first massive black holes, yet their evolution remains poorly understood at extreme masses. Using GENEC, we evolve rotating zero metallicity models from $500$ to $1000\,M_\odot$ at $v/v_{\rm crit}=0.1$ through core Si burning, and a $1000\,M_\odot$, $v/v_{\rm crit}=0.4$ model evolved through He exhaustion. In the fiducial $1000\,M_\odot$ model, convection and rotational transport carry freshly synthesized C and O into H burning layers, producing $62.1\,M_\odot$ of primary N by He exhaustion. Surface mass loss removes $20.2\,M_\odot$, including $1.8\times10^{-3}\,M_\odot$ of N, with $\log(\mathrm{N}/\mathrm{O})=0.68$, $\log(\mathrm{N}/\mathrm{C})=1.48$, and $\log(\mathrm{C}/\mathrm{O})=-0.80$. By the final hydrostatic model, the inner $100\,M_\odot$ is confined within $0.088\,R_\odot$ while the photosphere remains several thousand solar radii away. As C, Ne, O, and Si burning accelerate, chemical mixing freezes out and advanced products remain buried beneath the envelope. At core Si exhaustion, the central angular velocity reaches $4\times10^{-3}\,{\rm s^{-1}}$ while the surface rotates at $5.25\times10^{-8}\,{\rm s^{-1}}$, a contrast of $7.6\times10^4$. Contraction drives this spin up, while inner specific angular momentum changes by less than $1\%$. The maximum $j_{\rm eq}/j_{\rm ISCO}$ is $0.313$, limiting disk formation in our inside out estimate. These models show that Pop~III stars can produce strong primary N signatures and rapidly rotating black hole progenitors while their envelopes determine which products enrich the early Universe.

item.title: Scaling Up: A Global Optical/X-ray Correlation For Reprocessing Across Black Hole Masses
item.description: arXiv:2610.17248v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: This study extends the optical/X-ray correlation from black hole low-mass X-ray binaries (XRBs) to active galactic nuclei (AGN), bridging scales from stellar-mass to supermassive black holes (SMBHs). In XRBs, optical emission predominantly originates from the thermal reprocessing of high-energy photons on the surface of the geometrically thin, optically thick accretion disk. The reprocessed optical luminosity follows a power-law relation of the form $L_{V} \propto L_{X}^{\beta} a$, with $\beta \sim 0.5$, where $L_X$ is the X-ray luminosity and the orbital separation $a$ serves as a proxy for the disk size. To test the universality of this relationship across all mass scales, we analyzed quasi-simultaneous X-ray and optical flux data from a sample of XRBs and AGN that have estimates of the radius of the optically emitting disk. To bridge the structural differences between these populations, we utilized the characteristic optical/X-ray time lag derived from reverberation mapping as a physical proxy for the reprocessing radius. Our analysis reveals a tight, global correlation across all black hole masses, described by $\log L_V = 0.48\log L_X + 0.96\log a_R + 6.5$ with a scatter of $\sim 0.20$ dex, where $a_R$ is the reprocessing radius derived from the lag. Incorporating a geometric correction for the disk inclination angle ($\cos i$) slightly reduces this scatter to $0.18$ dex. These results suggest that X-ray reprocessing is scale-invariant across accretion disks, from stellar-mass black holes to SMBHs. This scaling relation provides new constraints for models of X-ray emission regions in accreting black holes.

item.title: An upper limit on Galactic OB+black hole binaries from SDSS-V
item.description: arXiv:2610.17253v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Binaries composed of a luminous OB star and a black hole (BH) are a key evolutionary link between massive stellar binaries and merging compact-object binaries, but only a handful are known and their occurrence fraction remains poorly constrained. We use multi-epoch spectroscopy from the SDSS-V Milky Way Mapper to place a first rigorous empirical upper limit on the fraction of Galactic massive ($\geq 10\,\mathrm{M}_\odot$) OB stars with a close BH companion, $f_\mathrm{BH}$. Radial-velocity (RV) variability alone cannot distinguish BH companions from the far more numerous luminous binaries. We therefore combine the SDSS-V RV variability measurements of 3130 massive OB stars with high-resolution follow-up and literature information to identify luminous companions among the RV-variable subset. Forward-modelling the detectability of OB+BH systems using BH masses and orbital parameters from binary-evolution models, we find $f_\mathrm{BH} \lesssim 3\%$ at 95% credibility. This empirical upper limit approaches, but does not exclude, theoretical predictions for the OB+BH fraction. The constraint is primarily limited by the number of RV-variable systems that can be decisively classified, highlighting the importance of complete, high-quality follow-up for future searches.

item.title: Henrietta Leavitt's classical Cepheid relation
item.description: arXiv:2610.17415v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: The Leavitt & Pickering (1912) mean period-magnitude relation for SMC Cepheids exhibits correlated residuals relative to modern Gaia $B_G$ and Johnson $V$ photometry ($r_{\delta V/\delta L12}\approx0.76$). Therefore dispersion inherent to Leavitt's photographic photometry relation is not solely random scatter ($\sigma_{L12,B_G,V}=0.22\pm0.03,0.25\pm0.04,0.20\pm0^{m}.03$), and is potentially consistent with the partial encoding of combined effects from the elongated SMC, classical Cepheid instability strip, differential reddening, etc. OGLE data indicate that $\gtrsim870$ SMC variables identified by Leavitt (1908, Table 2) are classical Cepheids ($\gtrsim 90$ %), and the preliminary unphased Table 2 photometry likewise features correlated residuals relative to contemporary observations ($r_{\delta B_G/\delta L08-T2}\approx0.54$). Table 6 data in Leavitt (1908, $n=16$) define a highly linear Leavitt law over an extensive baseline ($r\approx-0.98$), but constitute a smaller sample than the later 1912 work ($n=25$).

item.title: IC 1297: The Most Distant Known X-ray Planetary Nebula and One of the Most Luminous
item.description: arXiv:2610.17741v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We present the first targeted Einstein Probe (EP) X-ray observations of any planetary nebula (PN). Using the onboard Follow-up X-ray Telescope (FXT), we detect X-ray emission within the central region of IC 1297. The spectral analysis yields a plasma temperature of $kT = 0.086^{+0.054}_{-0.058}$ keV ($T\sim1.0 \times 10^{6}$ K), characteristic of shocked wind bubbles in PNe, whereas there is no evidence that its Wolf-Rayet central star emits X-rays. The absorption-corrected X-ray luminosity in the 0.3--2.0 keV energy band is $L_{\mathrm{X}} = 2.8 \times 10^{32}$ erg s$^{-1}$, also consistent with a hot bubble. At an adopted distance of $\sim3.8$ kpc, IC 1297 is the most distant X-ray emitting PN found to date, opening up a new observational window on hot-bubble formation and evolution. It is also among the most luminous known X-ray-emitting PNe. Our results demonstrate the capability of the EP FXT for detecting and characterizing faint, extended X-ray sources in the soft X-ray band for distant PNe, extending the known spectral properties of detectable X-ray emitting PNe. We also compiled the X-ray properties of all 41 known Galactic XPNe, finding a clear correlation between distance and X-ray luminosity that reflects an observational bias toward detecting the brightest sources at large distances. The compilation also shows a separation in X-ray luminosity between hot bubbles powered by H-rich and [WR]-type central stars, with the latter reaching luminosities up to an order of magnitude higher. The ten most luminous XPNe all host [WR]/PG 1159 central stars.

item.title: Low-frequency spectra and scattering of pulsars towards the Gum Nebula with the MWA
item.description: arXiv:2610.18146v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Context. The Gum Nebula is a nearby ionised complex with sight-line-dependent pulsar propagation. Aims. We test whether a smooth ionised structure can explain low-frequency spectral turnovers and pulse broadening, or whether smaller-scale material is required. Methods. We analysed Murchison Widefield Array observations of six pulsars at 80--240 MHz, combining sub-band flux densities with literature data. We compared power-law, free--free absorption (FFA), and turnover-constrained broken-power-law (BPL) spectra, and modelled scattering through pulse-profile convolution. PSR J0820-4114 and the Vela pulsar were fitted jointly across frequency. Results. All six spectra depart from a single power law. FFA is favoured for PSRs J0737-3039A and J0820-4114, and BPL for J0742-2822 and J0835-4510; the other two classifications depend on assumed error floors. Conditional FFA solutions imply emission measures of $10^4$--$10^5$ pc cm$^{-6}$ for electron temperatures of $3\times10^3$--$10^4$ K, far exceeding smooth-shell expectations. PSRs J0737-3039A and J0837-4135 have scattering laws consistent with $\tau_{\rm sc}\propto\nu^{-4}$. We obtain $\alpha_{\rm sc}=-3.07\pm0.11$ for J0742-2822 and $-1.59\pm0.44$ for J0820-4114 using a joint two-component model. The Vela pulsar is best described by an effective thick-screen model with $\alpha_{\rm sc}\simeq-2.74$. Neither tested Galactic electron-density model reproduces both independent distances and low-frequency scattering uniformly. Conclusions. The results favour a structured Gum--Vela magneto-ionic environment in which neighbouring sight lines probe different absorbing and scattering material; these effects need not arise in the same plasma component.

item.title: Extrapolating Collisional Rate Coefficients for Molecules of Astrophysical Interest Using Neural Networks
item.description: arXiv:2610.18278v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: State-to-state rate coefficients for inelastic molecular collisions are essential inputs for non-local thermodynamic equilibrium radiative transfer models, yet their computation using quantum scattering methods is prohibitive for large molecules and highly excited rotational states. We investigate the ability of artificial neural networks to extend existing datasets of collisional excitation rate coefficients without performing additional scattering calculations. A multilayer perceptron model was trained using molecular quantum numbers, level energies, energy gaps, and kinetic temperature as descriptors, and optimized on logarithmic rate coefficients. The model was tested on diverse collision systems ranging from simple diatomic molecules (CO, SiO) to open-shell species (SO), small asymmetric tops (H$_2$O, SO$_2$), and complex organic molecules (benzonitrile and vinyl cyanide) colliding with H$_2$ molecules or He atoms. Extrapolations were performed toward higher rotational levels, higher temperatures, and combinations of both. For most systems, predictions of rate coefficients involving previously unseen rotational states yielded mean error factors between 1.1 and 1.5, with the dominant rate coefficients generally reproduced more accurately than weaker transitions. Temperature extrapolations proved particularly successful, while combined extrapolations in temperature and rotational levels remained accurate to within a factor of two in most cases. The prediction quality depends on the interplay between dataset size, temperature range, molecular complexity, and the presence of clear collisional propensity rules. Overall, the approach demonstrates that machine learning can provide a practical route to extending collisional datasets for astrophysical applications, especially for large molecules for which additional quantum-scattering calculations are computationally demanding.

item.title: Delving into the depths of NGC 3783 with XRISM VI. Evidence for a failed wind based on Fe xxv absorption line variability
item.description: arXiv:2610.18429v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: NGC 3783 exhibits a prominent Fe XXV absorption trough in the time-averaged XRISM/Resolve spectrum. To investigate its short-term variability, we present a time-resolved analysis of the Fe XXV absorption line during the continuous 10-day observation. We divided the resolved absorption profile into five fixed velocity intervals and measured their normalized equivalent widths in 19 time-resolved spectra. Three velocity intervals exhibit significant equivalent-width (EW) variability. Two velocity intervals respond differently to low- and high-flux states with less emission line contamination. The time-dependent photoionisation modelling is unable to reproduce the most significant observed EW variation ($3.5 \, \sigma$), possibly owing to uncertainties in the assumed initial equilibrium state, which prevent a precise density measurement. Instead, using photoionisation calculations and assuming the high-density limit, we derive approximate constraints on the ionisation parameters of the two relevant components. The low-velocity component (-320 to -680 km/s) shows a delayed inverse response, indicating a high ionisation parameter, while its relatively short lag timescale indicates a relatively high density and a distance upper limit of 0.05 pc. In contrast, the high-velocity component (-680 to -1040 km/s) manifests a positive response with a longer lag to the ionising continuum, implying a relatively low ionisation parameter. This component appears to be less dense, with an inferred distance upper limit of 0.25 pc. The low-velocity component is consistent with a failed wind, as its outflow velocity is below the local escape velocity, whereas the high-velocity component lies near the escape threshold. Together with the lower-ionisation failed wind detected in 2001, this supports a multiphase failed-wind scenario in the unobscured state of NGC~3783 over more than two decades.

item.title: Broadband non-thermal emission predictions based on 3D simulations of supernova explosions within active galactic nuclei jets
item.description: arXiv:2610.18476v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Thermonuclear and core-collapse supernovae are statistically expected to happen within extragalactic jets, as these jets cross the inner regions of their host galaxies, and supernova ejecta-jet interactions can potentially lead to strong non-thermal activity. We model the non-thermal emission from a supernova interacting with a jet on kiloparsec scales, using detailed numerical simulations of the interaction. Using a post-processing method, we applied a non-thermal model of the acceleration and transport of electron and their synchrotron and inverse Compton emissions, simplified and tuned for flexibility and computational speed, to the results of a three-dimensional relativistic hydrodynamics simulation of the ejecta of a supernova interacting with an extragalactic jet. For intermediate jet powers, radio, optical and X-ray fluxes from supernova ejecta-jet interactions may be detectable for distances < 100Mpc. The non-thermal luminosity budget and local conditions associated with these interactions could be enough to explain knots seen in kiloparsec scale jets at different energies. These conditions might also be suitable for the production of heavy ultra high-energy cosmic rays, but photon and neutrino generation from hadronic processes would be minor on kiloparsec scales. The leptonic gamma-ray fluxes are modest but might non-negligibly contribute in TeV for the nearest or more powerful jet sources.

item.title: The ePESSTO+ census of ZTF nuclear transients. I. What flares in galactic nuclei?
item.description: arXiv:2610.18633v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Transients in galactic nuclei arise from distinct processes, only some of which trace the supermassive black hole (SMBH). These include tidal disruption events (TDEs), changing-look active galactic nuclei, Bowen fluorescence flares (BFFs) and ambiguous nuclear transients, alongside supernovae that appear nuclear but are unrelated to the SMBH. Reliable classification requires spectroscopy, which will not scale to the alert volumes of the Legacy Survey of Space and Time (LSST). We aim to characterise the population of nuclear transients, to identify early observables capable of distinguishing SMBH-related flares, and TDEs in particular, from the dominant supernova background, and to assess the biases this selection introduces. We implemented a real-time filter on the Lasair broker, selecting transients from the Zwicky Transient Facility (ZTF) alert stream by nuclear coincidence with the host galaxy, with no photometric cuts, to retain SMBH-related flares in both quiescent and active hosts. The filter ran over 16 months, with candidates reported for classification through ePESSTO+ and other facilities. The filter returned 476 candidates, of which 202 were spectroscopically classified, yielding predominantly supernovae, 10 confirmed TDEs (5%) and one BFF. The mean g-r colour and the rise time separate TDEs from the supernova background. Our filter recovers 10 of the 25 TDEs classified in the same period and declination range; most misses are technical or observational rather than physical. Simple real-time filtering combined with basic photometric criteria can already isolate TDEs efficiently from nuclear transient alert streams, and high completeness is achievable. In the LSST era, where samples will be predominantly photometric, selection bias will become as important as contamination, and retaining flares in active hosts is necessary if unusual events are not to be excluded.

item.title: Anchoring the Chromospheric Activity$-$Rotation Relation: A Study of the Pleiades and Group X
item.description: arXiv:2610.18644v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We present a study of the rotation and the chromospheric H$\alpha$ activity of low-mass stars in the $\approx$120 Myr-old Pleiades and the $\approx$400 Myr-old Group X open clusters. We combine published and new rotation periods ($P_\mathrm{rot}$) from TESS and ZTF, and use LAMOST, SDSS, and MDM spectra to measure H$\alpha$ equivalent widths (EWs). While overall the Group X distributions of $P_\mathrm{rot}$ and EWs are as expected, detailed comparisons to the Pleiades and to the 700-Myr-old benchmark Praesepe produce some surprises. For F through mid K stars, the Group X color$-$period sequence lies between those of the Pleiades and of Praesepe, as expected. But the $P_\mathrm{rot}$ for its late K and early M dwarfs and the Praesepe slow-rotator sequence overlap, indicating that the 700 Myr-old stars have not spun down significantly despite being nearly twice as old as their Group X counterparts. In the Rossby number$-L_\mathrm{H\alpha}/L_\mathrm{bol}$ plane, rapid rotators in Group X are saturated, as is seen in older clusters, whereas the rapid rotators in the Pleiades show a weak but measurable dependence of $L_\mathrm{H\alpha}/L_\mathrm{bol}$ on rotation. This implies that the chromospheric activity$-$rotation relation attains its mature form between 120 and 400 Myr. Dividing the sample by color reveals that K, M0, and M1 dwarfs are no longer saturated by $\approx$120 Myr, M2 and M3 dwarfs become unsaturated between $\approx$400 and $\approx$700 Myr, and later M dwarfs remain largely saturated through field ages even as their saturated $L_\mathrm{H\alpha}/L_\mathrm{bol}$ levels decline, indicating that chromospheric evolution is not determined by rotation period alone.

item.title: Beneath the Surface: >85% of z>5.9 QSOs in Massive Host Galaxies are UV-Faint
item.description: arXiv:2506.24128v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We use [CII] observations of a large quasi-stellar object (QSO) sample to segregate sources by host galaxy mass, aiming to identify those in the most massive hosts. [CII] luminosity, a known tracer of molecular gas, is taken as a proxy for host mass and used to rank 190 QSOs at z>5.9, spanning a 6-mag UV luminosity range (-22<Muv<-28). Particularly valuable are Atacama Large Millimeter Array (ALMA) data from a cycle-10 program, providing [CII] coverage for 46 UV-faint (M_{UV,AB}>-24.5) and 25 especially UV-faint (Muv>-23.5) QSOs, improving statistics by 5x and 6x, respectively. Taking massive host galaxies to be those where L[CII]>1.8x10^9 Lsol (median L[CII] of UV-bright QSOs), we identify 61 QSOs, including 13 which are UV-faint and 7 especially UV-faint. Using these selections and recent QSO luminosity functions (LFs), we present the first characterization of UV luminosity distribution for QSOs in massive host galaxies and quantify [CII] LFs for both UV-bright and UV-faint QSOs. While ~3% of massive-host QSOs are UV-bright (Muv<-26), >~85% are UV-faint (Muv>-24.5). This wide dispersion in UV luminosities reflects variations in dust obscuration, accretion efficiency, and black hole mass. Though spectroscopy is needed for definitive conclusions, black hole mass appears to be the dominant factor driving variations in the UV luminosity, based on 34 [CII]-luminous (L[CII]>1.8x10^9 Lsol) QSOs distributed across a ~3-mag baseline in UV luminosity and with measured MBH. At Muv~-23, the median extrapolated log10 (MBH/Msol) is 8.1+/-0.4, consistent with the local relation. Supermassive black holes (SMBHs) in UV-bright QSOs thus appear to be ~15(-9)(+25)x more massive than typical for massive host galaxies at z~6.

item.title: The Nineteenth Data Release of the Sloan Digital Sky Survey
item.description: arXiv:2507.07093v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Mapping the local and distant Universe is key to our understanding of it. For decades, the Sloan Digital Sky Survey (SDSS) has made a concerted effort to map millions of celestial objects to constrain the physical processes that govern our Universe. The most recent and fifth generation of SDSS (SDSS-V) is organized into three scientific ``mappers". Milky Way Mapper (MWM) that aims to chart the various components of the Milky Way and constrain its formation and assembly, Black Hole Mapper (BHM), which focuses on understanding supermassive black holes in distant galaxies across the Universe, and Local Volume Mapper (LVM), which uses integral field spectroscopy to map the ionized interstellar medium in the local group. This paper describes and outlines the scope and content for the nineteenth data release (DR19) of SDSS and the most substantial to date in SDSS-V. DR19 is the first to contain data from all three mappers. Additionally, we also describe nine value added catalogs (VACs) that enhance the science that can be conducted with the SDSS-V data. Finally, we discuss how to access SDSS DR19 and provide illustrative examples and tutorials.

item.title: Deep XMM-Newton observation reveals hot gaseous outflow in NGC 5746
item.description: arXiv:2510.00868v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We present a deep XMM-Newton observation of the massive, edge-on galaxy NGC 5746. The total exposure time of 250 ks provides unprecedented sensitivity to study the diffuse hot gas in the halo, significantly surpassing the depth of previous observations. While the presence of hot, circumgalactic gas is well tested for starburst galaxies, detections in normal galaxies remain scarce. By studying the diffuse X-ray emission in NGC 5746, we aim to provide new insights into the evolution of star-forming galaxies and their surroundings. We create X-ray images and surface brightness profiles to quantify the distribution of extraplanar gas in the halo of NGC 5746. In addition, we isolate the diffuse emission component from point source- and background-contamination and study the spectral characteristics of the hot plasma. We detect soft X-ray emission out to 40 kpc from the galactic disc. The gas distribution is reminiscent of a stellar outflow, with two bubbles extending perpendicular to the disc in a biconical shape. The spectral analysis of the halo emission yields a plasma temperature of 0.56 keV, higher than the typical values observed in spiral galaxies (0.2 keV). The disc has an even higher plasma temperature of 0.7 keV, and is dominated by non-thermal emission from unresolved X-ray binaries. The signs of a stellar outflow, bright X-ray emission, and high plasma temperatures indicate that the star-forming activity in NGC 5746 might be higher than previously thought. Our results demonstrate that massive spiral galaxies can host luminous X-ray halos, and support theoretical models that predict their existence. Earlier claims of a lack of hot gas around quiescent spirals might be attributed to the detection thresholds in shallower observations, stressing the need for more, deeper observations of non-starburst galaxies.

item.title: Mergers lighting the early Universe: modest star formation enhancement without evidence for AGN or Ly$\alpha$ triggering
item.description: arXiv:2510.14743v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Galaxy mergers and interactions are often invoked to explain enhanced star formation, black hole growth, and mass build-up of galaxies at later cosmic times, but their effect is poorly understood at high redshift ($z>2$). We use JADES data to analyse a mass-complete sample of 1968 galaxies at $z=3-9$ with ${\rm log}(M_\star/{\rm M_\odot}) = [8, 10]$, identifying major merger pairs (projected separation of $5-100$ pkpc, mass ratio $\geq 1/4$) using a probabilistic method. To look for signatures of enhancement in multiple physical properties, we carefully build a control sample of non-pairs that are simultaneously matched in redshift, stellar mass, isolation, and environment to the pair sample. We find a moderate enhancement in specific star-formation rate (sSFR) of a factor of $1.10\pm 0.05$ at separations $\lesssim 20$ kpc in pairs compared to their matched controls. We find that the interaction-related sSFR enhancement is most apparent at longer SFR averaging time-scales (50-100 Myr), whereas the enhancement is not detected on 5-10 Myr time-scales, where bursty star formation might be driven by internal processes. By averaging star formation histories, we find two distinct populations: one with monotonically rising SFRs and another with an earlier peak in SFR, potentially corresponding to different interaction stages. Finally, we find no significant excess of AGN in pairs, consistent with galaxy interactions not strongly triggering black hole activity at the separations probed ($>5$ kpc). Similarly, we also do not detect an excess in the fraction of Lyman-$\alpha$ emitters in pairs, suggesting that at the probed separations, galaxy interactions are not efficient at enhancing Lyman-$\alpha$ photon production and escape, which may only become important at the smallest physical scales.

item.title: Danger Zone: Establishing Buffers for Enhanced Classification in BPT Diagrams
item.description: arXiv:2512.07975v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: This study utilizes unsupervised machine learning, specifically the uniform manifold approximation and projection (UMAP) algorithm, to classify optical spectra originating from star-forming regions, Seyferts, and low-ionization (nuclear) emission-line regions (LI(N)ERs) based on their line ratios. Typically, the ionization source of a region is determined from intensity ratio of different combinations of pairs of spectral lines. However, using current boundary definitions, $\sim10$\% of spectra change classes between diagnostic diagrams. We apply the machine learning technique to $\sim$1.3 million optical spectra from 6,439 galaxies observed in the MaNGA survey. By training UMAP on consistently classified data, we can classify these ``ambiguous'' spectra, and delineate boundary zones where such ambiguities arise. Furthermore, we identify physically interesting subsets within the ambiguous spectra. Future work will incorporate additional parameters, such as alternative emission line ratios and velocity dispersions, to enhance classification accuracy.

item.title: Learning to See Sharper: A Physics-Informed Artificial Intelligence Framework for Super-Resolving Galaxy Spectra
item.description: arXiv:2603.18357v4 Announce Type: replace Abstract: The information recoverable from galaxy spectra depends fundamentally on spectral resolution, yet assembling large samples at high resolution remains observationally expensive. We present a deep-learning framework for spectral super-resolution that enhances low-resolution galaxy spectra by a factor of $\sim$10 in resolving power ($R\sim100$ to $R\sim1000$). The model is trained on 2,858 paired JWST/NIRSpec observations from the JADES program, where low-resolution prism spectra are matched with medium-resolution grating spectra (G140M, G235M, G395M) combined into a unified reference covering $1.0-5.3\mu\mathrm{m}$. Our three-stage architecture performs an initial super-resolution, infers the redshift from the coarse reconstruction, and then applies a physics-informed residual refinement that uses attention across emission-line tokens to learn inter-line relationships and predict parametric line profiles, alongside a convolutional branch for continuum corrections. Evaluated on a 20% held-out sample, the model achieves noise-limited residuals over most of the spectral range and improves the signal-to-noise ratio of key diagnostic lines including [OII], H$\beta$, [OIII], and H$\alpha$. The super-resolved spectra separate features that are entirely unresolved at prism resolution, such as the [OIII] $\lambda\lambda4959,5007$ doublet and H$\beta$, in exchange for a modest retrieval of line fluxes. As a proof of concept using JWST data, this approach is readily extensible to the low-resolution grism spectroscopy that will be delivered by Euclid and the Roman Space Telescope, potentially enabling population-level diagnostics across millions of galaxy spectra that would otherwise be inaccessible at low-resolution.

item.title: Global m=1 slow mode in near-Keplerian self-gravitating torus: applications to stellar nuclear disks and AGN molecular tori
item.description: arXiv:2604.11528v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Global m=1 asymmetries are observed in many self-gravitating astrophysical systems and are often interpreted as large-scale slow modes in near-Keplerian potentials. Prominent examples include eccentric nuclear disks in galactic centres, such as the double nucleus of M31. However, the origin and long-term stability of such modes remain unclear. We investigate the evolution and stability of a collisionless, self-gravitating torus orbiting a dominant central mass, aiming to determine whether a slow non-axisymmetric (m=1) mode can arise spontaneously. We perform direct N-body simulations exploring different torus-to-central mass ratios and initial conditions. The calculations use the high-order Hermite GPU integrator ($\varphi$-GPU), allowing us to follow long-term evolution with many particles. We find that a global slow m=1 mode forms spontaneously from initially axisymmetric configurations. The lopsided structure is sustained by coherent apsidal alignment and persists over secular timescales. Its maintenance requires nonlinear coupling of low-order modes, including the m=3 component, as well as a sufficient vertical thickness of the torus. As a result of the long-lived overdensity, the central mass is displaced from the system barycenter. These results provide a framework for understanding eccentric nuclear disks, such as those in M31 and NGC4486B, as well as molecular tori in AGNs, and suggest that such asymmetries may produce observable offsets of the central supermassive black hole.

item.title: Witnessing the Earliest Phases of Galactic Wind Formation in Superluminous Supernova Hosts: Implications for Star-formation-driven Outflows in Low- and High-redshift Galaxies
item.description: arXiv:2604.13865v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Direct observational constraints on the earliest phases of galactic outflows remain scarce. We present Very Large Telescope/X-shooter spectroscopy of seven Type I superluminous supernova (SLSN-I) host galaxies at $z = 0.15 - 0.51$, exploiting the bright SLSN continua as down-the-barrel probes of the host interstellar medium. Five of the seven hosts exhibit narrow, blueshifted MgII $\lambda\lambda$2796,2803 absorption, indicative of the presence of low-ionized outflows. Voigt modeling of the MgII absorption yields bulk outflow velocities of $45-99 {\rm ~km~s^{-1}}$ and terminal velocities of $v_{\rm max} \simeq 103-164 {\rm ~km~s^{-1}}$ the latter being below the ones reported for more evolved galaxies of similarly low mass and star formation rate. Given the expected short lifetimes of massive SLSN progenitors, we argue that these outflows are most naturally explained as originating during the preceding stellar-wind-dominated phase. We derive wind masses of $M_{\rm wind} \simeq 10^{4}-10^{5} M_{\odot}$, mass outflow rates comparable to or lower than the star formation rates, and kinetic energies of $10^{51}-10^{52}$ erg. These energies represent only a modest fraction ($\simeq 10\%$) of the mechanical energy expected from stellar winds during the first few Myr, demonstrating that the observed outflows can be powered entirely by pre-supernova feedback. Together with their low terminal velocities, these results support a scenario in which stellar winds and radiation pressure dominate the early acceleration of cold outflows, before core-collapse supernovae become dynamically important. Our work provides one of the first empirical constraints on early feedback phases relevant for high-redshift galaxies and for time-dependent implementations of stellar feedback in galaxy formation simulations.

item.title: Cosmic evolution of the [CII]-to-dense neutral gas relation
item.description: arXiv:2604.19529v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: The [CII] 158 $\mu$m line is widely used to trace star formation and the gas contents of high-redshift galaxies. However, it remains unclear under which physical conditions it reliably traces the molecular reservoir, and whether a unique conversion factor $\alpha_{\rm [CII]}$ can be applied across cosmic time. We investigated the evolution of the relation between the [CII] luminosity and dense neutral gas mass from $z\simeq10$ to $z\simeq0.2$ using the Vintergatan simulation, a high-resolution cosmological zoom-in of a Milky Way-like galaxy. We post-processed the snapshots with the SKIRT radiative transfer code to generate synthetic [CII] data cubes. We measured global and spatially resolved (100 pc) relations between [CII] luminosity ($L_{\rm [CII]}$), star formation rate (SFR), and dense neutral gas mass ($M_{\rm DN}$). We followed the redshift evolution of the [CII]-to-molecular gas conversion factor $\alpha_{\rm [CII]}$, and link these trends to the evolution of the interstellar medium (ISM) phases. The global $L_{\rm [CII]}$-$M_{\rm DN}$ and $L_{\rm [CII]}$-SFR relations evolve from a steep, [CII]-deficient regime at very low metallicity to an almost linear behaviour, similar to calibrations at $z\approx2$, once the ISM reaches $Z \gtrsim 0.05$-$0.1\,Z_\odot$ at $z\lesssim5$. Over this evolution, $\alpha_{\rm [CII]}$ spans nearly three orders of magnitude, from $\gtrsim 10^4$ down to $\approx10 \,\rm{M_\odot\,L_\odot^{-1}}$, even though the [CII] emission remains spatially correlated with the dense neutral gas. A unique, redshift-independent $\alpha_{\rm [CII]}$ therefore cannot recover dense neutral gas masses across the regimes we explored. [CII] remains a viable tracer of dense neutral gas at very high redshifts, but only when used with conversion factors that explicitly account for metallicity, ISM phase mix, and merger events.

item.title: Boundary-supported radial layering in Hoag-like ring galaxies
item.description: arXiv:2605.14725v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Clean Hoag-like ring galaxies are often characterized by an old compact central component, a depleted gap, and a detached outer ring. We identify a boundary-supported radial-layering mechanism in a shell-deformed Kepler control model. A compact inner boundary supplies the core state, while a localized effective shell deformation, interpreted as the reduced imprint of externally supplied material settled near a finite circularization radius, needs to create only an internal maximum and a subsequent outer minimum. These act as the gap barrier and ring-supporting well. The onset of this structure is organized by a saddle-node threshold of the critical-point equation. In a 10^4-point Monte Carlo scan, shell-localized boundary-supported candidates occupy finite parameter volume under the adopted priors, and none of the localized candidates contains an ordered interior minimum--maximum--minimum subsequence. The same branch gives a scale-free gap-to-ring interval overlapping representative ratios for Hoag's Object, UGC 4599, and PGC 1000714, but not for the environmentally processed comparison object JO171.

item.title: Learning the Universe with PRFM-vol: Introducing a new subgrid model for star formation in cosmological simulations
item.description: arXiv:2606.10022v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We introduce PRFM-vol, a new subgrid model for star formation in cosmological simulations that aims to increase the physical realism of cosmological simulations by leveraging results obtained with focused ISM simulations. We deploy a modified effective equation of state and calculate the star formation rate for each gas cell as a function of the ambient densities of gas, dark matter, and stars, based on the pressure-regulated feedback-modulated (PRFM) theory of star formation. Test simulations of our model in isolated galaxies show that we match PRFM predictions and TIGRESS scaling relations remarkably well, provided sufficiently high resolution is available. In particular, we are able to clearly demonstrate the impact of the stellar potential on the star formation rate, thereby retaining an important prediction of PRFM. We then apply our new model to cosmological multizoom simulations and find, compared to our previous TIGRESS/Schmidt model, a significant increase in the stellar scale heights and a slight increase in stellar mass. We demonstrate that modifying the effective equation of state significantly affects the morphology of simulated galaxies. Pronounced stellar clumps appear if the effective pressure at low hydrogen number densities is low, and disappear for higher pressure. We show that the formation of clumps is a result of Toomre instabilities, and conclude that simulated galaxy morphologies can be used to constrain effective equation of state models. Overall, our results establish PRFM-vol as a new self-consistent, physics-motivated subgrid model for star formation in high-resolution cosmological simulations.

item.title: The Lumina Project: Intergalactic Clumping and Recombination Sinks
item.description: arXiv:2606.18382v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Recombinations during the Epoch of Reionization are intrinsically inhomogeneous, with different regions of the intergalactic medium contributing unevenly depending on their density, temperature, ionization state, and spatial patchiness. We combine the high- and medium-resolution 95.5 cMpc Thesan-1 andh Thesan-2 runs with the significantly larger 500 cMpc Lumina simulation to measure clumping factors and recombination rates consistently across different resolutions and box sizes. We consider the standard ionized hydrogen clumping factor, $C_{\rm HII} \equiv \langle n_{\rm HII}^2\rangle/\langle n_{\rm HII}\rangle^2$, and a recombination-weighted clumping factor, $C_{\rm rec}$. Despite differences in resolution, volume, and reionization history, the simulations show an approximately universal clumping evolution at the 10-20% level when parametrized by the global ionized fraction $x_{\rm HII}$ rather than by redshift. Across all simulations, $C_{\rm rec}$ remains systematically below $C_{\rm HII}$, with the discrepancy increasing toward lower redshift as photoheating suppresses recombinations. In \lumina, the density-only prescription overpredicts the instantaneous recombination rate by factors of 1.29 at $z\approx8$ and 1.84 at $z\approx5$, and the cumulative recombination count by a factor of 1.45 by $z\approx5$. Mapping the recombination budget in the joint overdensity-temperature plane reveals that the dominant recombination ridges closely follow simple analytic thermal equilibrium bands. Finally, we introduce a phase-space recombination integral and define a phase-space clumping factor, $C_{\rm ps}(\Delta,T)$, which isolates the intrinsic recombination enhancement associated with ionization structure and thermal state at fixed overdensity and temperature.

item.title: Can third- and fourth-order multipoles plus radial variation of iso-density ellipses explain the observed flux ratios in B1422$+$231? YES, and a lesson learned from a TNG100 lensing galaxy sample
item.description: arXiv:2607.11559v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Flux ratio anomalies in multiply-imaged quasar lenses are a long-standing issue. Using a classical system B1422+231 as a case study, we investigate how typical non-clumpy perturbations beyond elliptical shapes -- multipoles $m_3, m_4$ and radial variations in $q, \phi_q$ -- can account for the observed image positions and flux ratios under different observational precisions. We extract these perturbations from a pre-selected strong-lensing galaxy sample from the TNG100 simulation. Smooth macroscopic models (SIE+$\gamma$, EPL+$\gamma$) are then fitted to the observed image positions alone and to both positions and flux ratios, with and without including the extracted perturbations. With astrometric uncertainty of $\sigma_{p}=10$ mas, both macro-models alone can already successfully fit image positions within $3\sigma_{p}$. At $\sigma_{p}=2$ mas, however, 'astrometric anomalies' appear if smooth macro-models alone are adopted. In this case, adding the extracted perturbations can explain the anomalous image positions. When both positions and flux ratios are adopted, the SIE+$\gamma$ model family already shows 'flux ratio anomalies' at photometric uncertainty $\sigma_{f} \le 10\%$ (keeping $\sigma_{p}=10$ mas). When EPL+$\gamma$ is used, the smooth model alone can simultaneously fit both positions and flux ratios with $\sigma_{f}=10\%, 5\%$, but not with $\sigma_{f}=2\%$, where 'flux ratio anomalies' appear. Adding all four types of extracted perturbations can rescue the macro-models and explain the observed anomalous flux ratios. We present important lessons learned regarding model flexibility and degeneracy.

item.title: Discrepancies between Chandrasekhar's theory of relaxation and $N$-body simulations
item.description: arXiv:2607.14844v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Globular clusters are systems which are known to be particularly well described by two-body relaxation. In recent decades many studies have shown that Chandrasekhar's orbit-averaged theory is able to reproduce many features of numerical simulations. However, it has been claimed that differences between the theory and simulation remain, such as an amplitude mismatch of the rate of change of the distribution function. In this paper we compare the theoretical predictions of Chandrasekhar's theory for anisotropic clusters to precise $N$-body data. We show that more careful $N$-body measurements are able to reduce the claimed mismatch. Nevertheless, we observe a dependency of the remaining mismatch on both position and anisotropy. While the dependence on anisotropy may be understood qualitatively on theoretical grounds, the radial dependence implies that spatial inhomogeneities, and therefore collective effects, may become unavoidable to resolve the residual mismatch between theory and simulations.

item.title: Star formation powers optical line emission from the CGM
item.description: arXiv:2607.18385v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Using integral field spectroscopy, we explore the disk-halo interface, or the inner circumgalactic medium (CGM), of individual galaxies by constructing and analyzing emission-line maps for a large sample (72) of normal, low-redshift galaxies spanning three orders of magnitude in stellar mass and four orders in star formation rate (SFR). We find a steep turnover occurring at $(1-2) R_e$ in the H$\alpha$, [O {\small II}], and [O {\small III}] line emission radial profiles. Beyond this radius, the slope of the line emission radial profiles becomes shallower as the SFR of the central galaxy decreases, which might reflect the strength of the feedback processes. The line emission fluxes at large radius ($(5-10) R_e$ or $\sim (0.1-0.25)r_{\rm vir}$) correlate with the galaxy's SFR, but not with its stellar mass. These findings suggest that ionizing photons escaping from star-forming regions in the central galaxy account for the observed emission line fluxes from the inner CGM, with escape fractions inferred from the [O {\small III}] and [O {\small II}] ratio. Different state-of-the-art theoretical models do not agree on the predicted dependence of cool gas on the SFR of the central galaxies, highlighting the importance of CGM emission line measurements to distinguish between different subgrid models for star formation and feedback processes.

item.title: Little Red Dots are Direct-Collapse Black Hole-Forming Galaxies
item.description: arXiv:2609.12049v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: "Little Red Dots" (LRDs) at $4 < z < 8$ are one of the most challenging discoveries by JWST to date because their distinctive V-shaped spectra and compact morphologies (100 - 200 pc) defy conventional astrophysical interpretation. Previous attempts to explain LRDs as compact stellar systems, heavily-cocooned black holes with differential flows, supermassive stars, or more exotic objects like 'black-hole stars' either cannot show how they formed, explain the origin of the dense shells needed for the absorption features in their spectra, or account for their observed abundances or inferred lifetimes. Here we show that LRDs are simply direct-collapse black hole galaxies in which the BH is still shrouded by the massive disk that created it. Our cosmological simulations yield spectra that are good matches to those of LRDs because high densities at the center of the disk trap X-rays from the BH and produce the observed Balmer absorption features while allowing UV, optical and reprocessed IR flux to partly escape. The host galaxy forms a dense 10$^8$ M$_{\odot}$ cluster of stars with a radius of 150 pc next to the BH, consistent with observations of LRDs. Our models reproduce a wide variety of LRD spectra from typical objects like RUBIES-EGS-42046 at $z = 5.28$ to those with the strongest Balmer breaks such as MoM-BH$^*$-1 at $z = 7.76$ and those at the highest redshifts like CAPERS-LRD-z9 at $z = 9.29$.

item.title: Resolved SED modelling with JWST and ALMA: the role of stellar mass surface density in regulating star formation in cosmic noon galaxies
item.description: arXiv:2609.12059v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We present kpc-scale ($0.2''-0.5''$) physical property maps of 35 main-sequence galaxies at $z \approx 0.5-3.7$, with stellar masses of $\log(M_*/M_\odot) \sim 9.7-11.7$ and star formation rates of $\mathrm{SFR} \sim 1.4-280\,\mathrm{M_\odot\,yr^{-1}}$, selected from the ALMA Spectroscopic Survey (ASPECS) in the Hubble Ultra Deep Field. Leveraging the unique HST, JWST (NIRCam and MIRI), and ALMA observations, we perform spatially resolved spectral energy distribution (SED) modeling across the UV-to-FIR regime. We find that incorporating MIRI and/or ALMA data reduces the overestimation of dust luminosity (by up to $\sim0.8$ dex), while ALMA observations further mitigate the age-dust degeneracy. In the absence of such data, restricting the SED model library based on the observed unresolved colors can partially mitigate these biases. The stellar masses ($M_{*}$) derived from resolved and unresolved modeling are consistent within $\sim0.05$ dex, suggesting that mass discrepancies (attributed to outshining) are less significant for cosmic noon main-sequence galaxies when rest-frame near-infrared (NIR; e.g., $\sim1-3\,\mu\mathrm{m}$) data are included. After normalization to the same reference, the composite SED of our sample closely resembles that of local starburst galaxies such as M82, suggesting similar dust attenuation and re-emission properties. Finally, we find that the molecular gas fraction and depletion time correlate with the effective stellar mass surface density ($\Sigma_{\rm eff,*} = M_{*}/2\pi R_{\rm eff,M_*}^2$) similarly to that observed in local galaxies. These results provide a first qualitative view of how the stellar gravitational potential influences gas regulation and star formation in galaxies beyond the local Universe.

item.title: A dense, metal-rich absorber driven by a heavily dust-obscured galaxy: The direct evidence of CGM enrichment at $z\sim7$
item.description: arXiv:2609.17680v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We report the serendipitous discovery of a dense, metal-enriched circumgalactic medium (CGM) absorber at z=7.03, together with its host galaxy, identified along the sightline toward a red quasar. The absorber exhibits the largest rest-frame equivalent widths and column densities observed to date at z>5, tracing a metal-enriched gaseous halo. Using deep JWST/NIRSpec and NOEMA observations, we characterize the absorber's physical properties and identify its host, ND1, as a vigorously star-forming galaxy at an exceptionally close impact parameter of ~16kpc, so heavily dust-obscured that it is detected only in the longest-wavelength NIRCam bands. Detections of [OIII]$\lambda$5007, H$\alpha$, and [CII]$\lambda 158\,\mu$m emission anchor the systemic redshift to z~7.0321, revealing a coherent ~50km/s blueshift of the absorbing gas relative to the host, suggesting outflow-driven metal transport into the halo. The outflow velocity, combined with the measured column density, implies an outflow rate of $\dot{M}_{\rm out}=64 M_\odot\,yr^{-1}$ and a mass loading factor $\eta=3$, indicating an energetic, chemically-enriched wind launched from a dust-obscured starburst. While the overall ionization state and [Mg/Fe] ratio align with empirical cosmic evolutionary trends, the absorber displays an enhanced carbon-to-oxygen ([C/O]) ratio. This abundance pattern suggests the nucleosynthetic yields of Population~III stellar explosions, and aligns with the host's star-formation history extending to $z \gtrsim 8$, potentially offering a rare fossil record of primordial metal enrichment. Our findings demonstrate that intense star-formation feedback can rapidly and efficiently pollute the CGM/IGM well into the Epoch of Reionization. The NIR-dark nature of the host further implies that rest-UV surveys may systematically miss the dusty sources that drive CGM- and IGM-scale metal enrichment in the early Universe.

item.title: Cosmic web Ly$\alpha$ emission in a sample of overdense regions
item.description: arXiv:2609.20938v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We present a complete and homogeneous analysis of the Ly$\alpha$ emission properties of the cosmic web at $3 \lesssim z \lesssim 5$ as a function of the overdensity of Ly$\alpha$ emitters (LAEs) in the MUSE Ultra Deep Field (MUDF) and the MUSE Extremely Deep Field (MXDF). We identify 41 overdensities, probing environments that are $\delta \approx 2 - 10$ times denser than the field. We search for extended emission down to surface brightness (SB) levels of $3 - 5 \times 10^{-20}\ \mathrm{erg\ s^{-1}\ cm^{-2}\ arcsec^{-2}}$, revealing filamentary structures beyond the scale of the circumgalactic medium, confirming that LAEs act as signposts of the cosmic web. A trend with overdensity emerges: non-detections are mainly at $\delta < 2$, a $\approx 1$ dex scatter in SB appears for $2 \lesssim \delta \lesssim 3.5$, and detections reach a maximum intrinsic SB of $\approx 2 \times 10^{-19}\ \mathrm{erg\ s^{-1}\ cm^{-2}\ arcsec^{-2}}$ for $\delta \gtrsim 3.5$. Emitting regions occupy a fraction of projected area $f_s \approx 0.20 - 0.25$ inside filaments, yielding a cosmological incidence for Ly$\alpha$ emission in the cosmic web $\ell(\mathrm{Ly}\alpha)$ of $\approx 1.22$, which is similar to the one of partially-neutral Lyman limit systems. This analysis indicates that the emitting gas is partially ionized at moderate densities ($n_{\mathrm{H}} \approx 10^{-3} - 10^{-1}\ \mathrm{cm}^{-3}$), likely tracing the denser spines of intergalactic filaments and embedded substructures. Finally, we forecast how oriented stacking in larger samples of overdensities from shallower observations could yield an expanded view of the cosmic web before the next-generation wide-field spectroscopic instruments become operational.

item.title: A 210 Megaparsec Ionized Structure at $z=6.8$ Revealed by an Astrophysics Foundation Model
item.description: arXiv:2609.36656v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Reionization is the last major transition in the Universe that transforms the intergalactic medium (IGM) from neutral to highly ionized, yet its spatial structure remains poorly constrained. Using an astrophysics foundation model trained for James Webb Space Telescope datasets, we identify a luminous galaxy at redshift $z=7.567$ showing significant Ly$\alpha$ transmission at $z=6.80\pm0.07$. This transmission, named ``the First Ly$\alpha$ transmission in the Reionization Epoch at $z\sim7$" (FL$\alpha$RE-z7), indicates a cosmological-scale ionized structure extending over $210.5^{+55.7}_{-53.5}$ comoving Megaparsecs at cosmic dawn. The hydrogen neutral fraction of the ionized structure is $x_{\rm HI}=(2.07^{+0.29}_{-0.30})\times10^{-6}$, about $10^5$ times lower than the cosmic mean at similar redshifts $(x_{\rm HI}\approx0.4)$. Cosmological simulations suggest a probability of $\approx10^{-5}$ for a random sightline to reproduce the transmission. We find no significant galaxy overdensity associated with the transmission region, in tension with canonical inside-out reionization models. FL$\alpha$RE-z7 severely challenges existing reionization models in the standard $\Lambda$CDM Universe, indicating extreme spatial fluctuation in ionizing radiation or IGM temperature. Our result marks the first example of a foundation model discovering a previously unpredicted astrophysical phenomenon, demonstrating the power of deep learning methods for mining large astronomical datasets and finding unexpected new astrophysics.
